7removed-- # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
8removed
9removed-- Note to developers (before next release):
10removed-- Needs some WORKINCLASSes and some quizzes

19removed--

21removed-- to this chapter (and into later files, as appropriate). We haven't done
22removed-- it yet because it's a shame to complicate the nice simple presentation
23removed-- here when it's used as the basis for applications like Xavier's static

26removed--
27removed-- MWH (port note): The Rocq chapter's "Rocq Automation" tour has been
28removed-- retooled here for Lean. The tactic combinators `try` and `repeat` (and
29removed-- the custom-tactic `macro`) are introduced in this chapter; `<;>` and
30removed-- `simp` were already introduced in Logical Foundations (`<;>` in
31removed-- `Induction`) so we use them freely and the `<;>` section below is a
32removed-- recap. For linear arithmetic we use `lia`; NOTE that LF currently

34removed-- volume-wide (either introduce `lia` in LF, or keep `omega`).
35removed
36removed-- In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a tool
37removed-- to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative programming
38removed-- language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of conventional
39removed-- mainstream languages such as C and Java.
40removed
41removed-- Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
42removed
43removed-- Z := X;
44removed-- Y := 1;
45removed-- while (Z ≠ 0) {
46removed-- Y := Y * Z;
47removed-- Z := Z - 1;
48removed-- }
49removed
50removed-- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp; later
51removed-- in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and introduce
52removed-- *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative programs.
53removed
54removed-- We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of *arithmetic
55removed-- and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter, *Slang*; read
56removed-- that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of arithmetic
57removed-- expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their evaluation
58removed-- both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive *relation* (proved
59removed-- equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program transformation together
60removed-- with its correctness proof. Those expressions are *variable-free*.
61removed
62removed-- This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
63removed-- *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
64removed-- conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
65removed
66removed-- ## Expressions With Variables
67removed
68removed-- Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich our
69removed-- arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things simple,
70removed-- we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only hold numbers.
71removed
72removed-- ### States
73removed
74removed-- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
75removed-- we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or just
76removed-- *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some point in
77removed-- the execution of a program.
78removed
79removed-- For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all* variables,
80removed-- even though any given program is only able to mention a finite number of
81removed-- them. Because each variable stores a natural number, we represent the state
82removed-- as a total map from strings (variable names) to `Nat`, and will use `0` as
83removed-- the default value in the store.
84removed
85removed-- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
86removed-- just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
87removed
88removedabbrev Ident := String
89removedabbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
90removed
91removed-- ### Syntax
92removed
93removed-- We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we had before simply by
94removed-- including one more constructor. (This is a fresh `Aexp`, replacing the
95removed-- variable-free one from the *Slang* chapter.)
96removed
97removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
98removed-- That should be a live chapter link.
99removed
100removedinductive Aexp where
101removed | num (n : Nat)
102removed | id (x : Ident) -- NEW
103removed | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
104removed | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
105removed | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
106removed
107removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
108removed-- Rather than define identifiers as Ident, a more general approach is to
109removed-- use a **type variable** with `DecidableEq` (as the `Maps` chapter
110removed-- does), threaded through `Aexp`/`Bexp`/`Com`/`State`. Stashed for a
111removed-- future decision; the parameterized version would look like:
112removed--
113removed-- `inductive Aexp (V : Type) where
114removed-- | num (n : Nat)
115removed-- | id (x : V)
116removed-- | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
117removed-- | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
118removed-- | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
119removed-- -- … then `Bexp V`, `Com V`, `abbrev State (V) [DecidableEq V] :=
120removed-- -- TotalMap V Nat`, and `[DecidableEq V]` wherever a lookup/update is
121removed-- -- performed.`
122removed
123removed-- The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now refers to the new
124removed-- `Aexp`.
125removed
126removedinductive Bexp where
127removed | bool (b : Bool)
128removed | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
129removed | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
130removed | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
131removed | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
132removed | not (b : Bexp)
133removed | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
134removed
135removed-- Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make examples easier to
136removed-- read.
137removed
138removeddef W : Ident := "W"
139removeddef X : Ident := "X"
140removeddef Y : Ident := "Y"
141removeddef Z : Ident := "Z"
142removed
143removed-- (This convention for naming program variables (`X`, `Y`, `Z`) clashes a bit
144removed-- with our earlier use of uppercase letters for types. Since we're not using
145removed-- polymorphism heavily in the chapters developed to Imp, this overloading
146removed-- should not cause confusion.)
147removed
148removed-- ### Notations
149removed
150removed-- To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some notations
151removed-- and implicit coercions.
152removed
153removed-- You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do. Briefly,
154removed-- though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
155removed
156removed-- - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
157removed-- grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals further
158removed-- below.
159removed
160removed-- - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there are
161removed-- eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`, as
162removed-- `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for building
163removed-- larger expressions, with some annotations to define precedence, etc.
164removed
165removed-- - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
166removed-- `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
167removed
168removed-- Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern exactly,
169removed-- so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open one if you want
170removed-- to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.
171removed
172removed/-- Arithmetic expressions of Imp -/
173removeddeclare_syntax_cat imp_aexp
174removed/-- Numeric literal -/
175removedsyntax:max num : imp_aexp
176removed/-- Variable reference -/
177removedsyntax:max ident : imp_aexp
178removed/-- Addition -/
179removedsyntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " + " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
180removed/-- Subtraction -/
181removedsyntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " - " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
182removed/-- Multiplication -/
183removedsyntax:70 imp_aexp:70 " * " imp_aexp:71 : imp_aexp
184removed/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
185removedsyntax "(" imp_aexp ")" : imp_aexp
186removed/-- Escape to Lean -/
187removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : imp_aexp
188removed
189removed/-- Embed an Imp arithmetic expression into a Lean term -/
190removedsyntax:min "aexp " "{" imp_aexp "}" : term
191removed
192removedopen Lean in
193removedmacro_rules
194removed | `(aexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp.num $(quote n.getNat))
195removed | `(aexp { $x:ident }) => `(Aexp.id $x)
196removed | `(aexp { ~$e }) => pure e
197removed | `(aexp { $a + $b }) => `(Aexp.plus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
198removed | `(aexp { $a - $b }) => `(Aexp.minus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
199removed | `(aexp { $a * $b }) => `(Aexp.mult (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
200removed | `(aexp { ($a) }) => `(aexp {$a})
201removed
202removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: boolean expressions
203removed
204removed/-- Boolean expressions of Imp -/
205removeddeclare_syntax_cat imp_bexp
206removed/-- Boolean literal (`true` or `false`) -/
207removedsyntax:max ident : imp_bexp
208removed/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
209removedsyntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " = " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
210removed/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
211removedsyntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≠ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
212removed/-- Less than or equal -/
213removedsyntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≤ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
214removed/-- Greater than -/
215removedsyntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " > " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
216removed/-- Boolean negation -/
217removedsyntax:70 "¬ " imp_bexp:70 : imp_bexp
218removed/-- Boolean conjunction -/
219removedsyntax:35 imp_bexp:36 " ∧ " imp_bexp:35 : imp_bexp
220removed/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
221removedsyntax "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_bexp
222removed/-- Escape to Lean -/
223removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : imp_bexp
224removed
225removed/-- Embed an Imp boolean expression into a Lean term -/
226removedsyntax:min "bexp " "{" imp_bexp "}" : term
227removed
228removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: boolean expressions, macro rules
229removed
230removedopen Lean in
231removedmacro_rules
232removed | `(bexp { $x:ident }) =>
233removed match x.getId with
234removed | `true => `(Bexp.bool true)
235removed | `false => `(Bexp.bool false)
236removed | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
237removed | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e
238removed | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp = $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.eq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
239removed | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≠ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.neq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
240removed | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≤ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.le (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
241removed | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp > $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.gt (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
242removed | `(bexp { ¬ $b:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.not (bexp {$b}))
243removed | `(bexp { $b1:imp_bexp ∧ $b2:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.and (bexp {$b1}) (bexp {$b2}))
244removed | `(bexp { ($b:imp_bexp) }) => `(bexp {$b})
245removed
246removed-- We make it a little easier to write Imp programs using normal constructors
247removed-- (i.e., without notation), by using *implicit coercions*. In Lean, a `Coe`
248removed-- instance tells the elaborator how to turn a value of one type into another
249removed-- automatically:
250removed
251removed-- - `Coe Ident Aexp` lets us write a bare variable (an `Ident`) where an `Aexp`
252removed-- is expected; the identifier is implicitly wrapped with `id`.
253removed
254removed-- - `OfNat Aexp n` lets us write a numeric literal where an `Aexp` is expected;
255removed-- it is implicitly wrapped with `num`.
256removed
257removed-- - `Coe Bool Bexp` lets us write a boolean literal (`true`/`false`) where a
258removed-- `Bexp` is expected; it is implicitly wrapped with `bool`.
259removed
260removedinstance : Coe Ident Aexp where
261removed coe := .id
262removed
263removedinstance (n : Nat) : OfNat Aexp n where
264removed ofNat := .num n
265removed
266removedinstance : Coe Bool Bexp where
267removed coe := .bool
268removed
269removed-- With these coercions we can write `.plus 3 (.mult X 2)` instead of the
270removed-- fully explicit `.plus (.num 3) (.mult (.id "X") (.num 2))`, and
271removed-- `.and true (.not …)` instead of `.and (.bool true) (.not …)`. More readably
272removed-- still, the concrete syntax from the Notations section lets us write these
273removed-- examples directly:
274removed
275removeddef example_aexp : Aexp := aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
276removeddef example_bexp : Bexp := bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }
277removed
278removed-- ### Delaborators
279removed
280removed-- The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
281removed-- `aexp
282removed-- { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
283removed-- using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
284removed-- `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
285removed-- *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax into a
286removed-- term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns an
287removed-- elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output uses our
288removed-- concrete Imp notation.
289removed
290removed-- Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the matching
291removed-- piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't recognize is
292removed-- printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute registers the
293removed-- top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to display a term headed
294removed-- by one of those constructors -- unless notation printing has been switched
295removed-- off with `set_option pp.notation false`, which lets us fall back to the raw
296removed-- constructors when debugging (see *Desugaring Notations* below). The
297removed-- companion *category parenthesizer* re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's
298removed-- precedences demand, so that, e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its
299removed-- parentheses intact.
300removed
301removed-- You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed below
302removed-- for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a proof goal
303removed-- mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp syntax rather
304removed-- than as a pile of constructors.
305removed
306removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing expressions back
307removed
308removednamespace Imp.Delab
309removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer
310removed
311removed/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
312removed@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
313removeddef imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
314removed maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
315removed parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
316removedwhere
317removed wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
318removed let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
319removed return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
320removed
321removed/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_bexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
322removed@[category_parenthesizer imp_bexp]
323removeddef imp_bexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
324removed maybeParenthesize `imp_bexp true wrapParens prec <|
325removed parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_bexp prec
326removedwhere
327removed wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
328removed let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
329removed return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
330removed
331removed/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
332removeddef annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
333removed (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
334removed
335removed/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
336removedpartial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
337removed let e ← getExpr
338removed let stx ←
339removed match_expr e with
340removed | Aexp.num _ =>
341removed match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
342removed | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
343removed | none => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
344removed | Aexp.id _ =>
345removed -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
346removed -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
347removed -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
348removed match ← withAppArg getExpr with
349removed | .const nm _ => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
350removed | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
351removed | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
352removed | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
353removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
354removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
355removed `(imp_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
356removed | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
357removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
358removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
359removed `(imp_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
360removed | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
361removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
362removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
363removed `(imp_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
364removed | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
365removed annAsTerm stx
366removed
367removed/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
368removedpartial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
369removed let e ← getExpr
370removed let stx ←
371removed match_expr e with
372removed | Bexp.bool _ =>
373removed match ← withAppArg getExpr with
374removed | .const ``Bool.true _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
375removed | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
376removed | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
377removed | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
378removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
379removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
380removed `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp = $s2:imp_aexp)
381removed | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
382removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
383removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
384removed `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≠ $s2:imp_aexp)
385removed | Bexp.le _ _ =>
386removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
387removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
388removed `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≤ $s2:imp_aexp)
389removed | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
390removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
391removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
392removed `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp > $s2:imp_aexp)
393removed | Bexp.not _ =>
394removed let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
395removed `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
396removed | Bexp.and _ _ =>
397removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
398removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
399removed `(imp_bexp| $s1 ∧ $s2)
400removed | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
401removed annAsTerm stx
402removed
403removed-- The `whenPPOption getPPNotation` wrapper lets
404removed-- `set_option pp.notation false` switch this delaborator off, revealing the
405removed-- raw constructors (see the "Desugaring Notations" discussion, after the
406removed-- commands are introduced).
407removed
408removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: registering the delaborators
409removed
410removed@[delab app.Aexp.num, delab app.Aexp.id, delab app.Aexp.plus,
411removed delab app.Aexp.minus, delab app.Aexp.mult]
412removedpartial def delabAexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
413removed -- This delaborator only understands `Aexp`'s constructors -- bail otherwise.
414removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
415removed | Aexp.num _ => true
416removed | Aexp.id _ => true
417removed | Aexp.plus _ _ => true
418removed | Aexp.minus _ _ => true
419removed | Aexp.mult _ _ => true
420removed | _ => false
421removed match ← delabAexpInner with
422removed | `(imp_aexp| ~$e) => pure e
423removed | e => `(term| aexp { $e })
424removed
425removed@[delab app.Bexp.bool, delab app.Bexp.eq, delab app.Bexp.neq, delab app.Bexp.le,
426removed delab app.Bexp.gt, delab app.Bexp.not, delab app.Bexp.and]
427removedpartial def delabBexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
428removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
429removed | Bexp.bool _ => true
430removed | Bexp.eq _ _ => true
431removed | Bexp.neq _ _ => true
432removed | Bexp.le _ _ => true
433removed | Bexp.gt _ _ => true
434removed | Bexp.not _ => true
435removed | Bexp.and _ _ => true
436removed | _ => false
437removed match ← delabBexpInner with
438removed | `(imp_bexp| ~$e) => pure e
439removed | e => `(term| bexp { $e })
440removed
441removedend Imp.Delab
442removed
443removed-- With these delaborators in place, Lean pretty-prints Imp expressions with
444removed-- the higher-level notations rather than their raw constructors.
445removed
446removed-- The pretty-printed version of an expression might not exactly match its
447removed-- original form. For example, the parentheses around `X * 2` in
448removed-- `aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }` are not printed because they are redundant -- which
449removed-- the parenthesizer knows.
450removed
451removed#check aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
452removed
453removed#check bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }
454removed
455removed-- ### Evaluation
456removed
457removed-- The arithmetic and boolean evaluators must now be extended to handle
458removed-- variables, taking a state `st` as an extra argument. A variable is looked
459removed-- up in the state with the map-indexing notation `st[x]` from the
460removed-- `Typeclasses` chapter. For the notation to work, we need to
461removed-- `open scoped MyGetElem`, which opens only the scoped items like notation
462removed-- from the module.
463removed
464removedopen scoped MyGetElem
465removed
466removeddef Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
467removed match a with
468removed | num n => n
469removed | id x => st[x] -- NEW
470removed | plus a1 a2 => a1.eval st + a2.eval st
471removed | minus a1 a2 => a1.eval st - a2.eval st
472removed | mult a1 a2 => a1.eval st * a2.eval st
473removed
474removeddef Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
475removed match b with
476removed | bool b => b
477removed | eq a1 a2 => a1.eval st == a2.eval st
478removed | neq a1 a2 => a1.eval st != a2.eval st
479removed | le a1 a2 => a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st
480removed | gt a1 a2 => a1.eval st > a2.eval st
481removed | not b1 => !b1.eval st
482removed | and b1 b2 => b1.eval st && b2.eval st
483removed
484removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
485removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
486removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
487removed (plus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st + a2.eval st := rfl
488removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
489removed (minus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st - a2.eval st := rfl
490removed@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
491removed (mult a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st * a2.eval st := rfl
492removed
493removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
494removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
495removed (eq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st == a2.eval st) := rfl
496removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
497removed (neq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st != a2.eval st) := rfl
498removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
499removed (le a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
500removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
501removed (gt a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st > a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
502removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
503removed@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b1 b2 : Bexp) :
504removed (and b1 b2).eval st = (b1.eval st && b2.eval st) := rfl
505removed
506removed-- We reuse the total-map notation (`x →ₜ v ; ∅` etc.) for states.
507removed
508removedexample : aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = 13 := by rfl
509removed
510removedexample : aexp { Z + (X * Y) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; Y →ₜ 4 ; ∅) = 20 := by rfl
511removed
512removedexample : bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = true := by rfl
513removed
514removed-- Note to developers:
515removed-- dsainati: Bikeshedding: I'm not sure how I feel about this arrow
516removed-- subscript for maps. Easy to change later but just flagging to discuss.
517removed-- mwhicks1: This comes from the Maps chapter, which chenson2018 is

520removed-- ## Commands
521removed
522removed-- Now we are ready to define the syntax and behavior of Imp *commands* (or
523removed-- *statements*). Informally, commands `c` are described by the following BNF
524removed-- grammar:
525removed
526removed-- c ::= skip
527removed-- | x := a
528removed-- | c ; c
529removed-- | if b then c else c end
530removed-- | while b do c end
531removed
532removed-- Here is the formal definition of the abstract syntax of commands.
533removed
534removedinductive Com where
535removed | skip
536removed | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
537removed | seq (c1 c2 : Com)
538removed | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
539removed | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
540removed
541removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: commands
542removed
543removed/-- Imp commands -/
544removeddeclare_syntax_cat imp_com
545removed
546removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: commands, macro rules
547removed
548removed/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
549removedsyntax ident ";" : imp_com
550removed/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
551removedsyntax imp_com ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
552removed/-- Assignment -/
553removedsyntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : imp_com
554removed/-- Conditional -/
555removedsyntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
556removed/-- Loop -/
557removedsyntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
558removed/-- Escape to Lean -/
559removedsyntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
560removed
561removed/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
562removedsyntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
563removed
564removedopen Lean in
565removedmacro_rules
566removed | `(imp { $x:ident ; }) =>
567removed if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
568removed else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
569removed | `(imp { $c1 $c2 }) =>
570removed `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
571removed | `(imp { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
572removed `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
573removed | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
574removed `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
575removed | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
576removed `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
577removed | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
578removed pure c
579removed
580removed-- Just as we did for expressions, we add a delaborator so that Lean prints
581removed-- commands back in the `imp { … }` concrete syntax (see the Delaborators
582removed-- section above). It reuses the expression delaborators for the condition of
583removed-- an `if`/`while` and for the right-hand side of an assignment, and prints an
584removed-- unrecognized subcommand with the `~` escape.
585removed
586removed-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing commands back
587removed
588removednamespace Imp.Delab
589removedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
590removed
591removed/-- Rebuild `imp_com` concrete syntax from a `Com` term. -/
592removedpartial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
593removed let e ← getExpr
594removed let stx ←
595removed match_expr e with
596removed | Com.skip => `(imp_com| skip;)
597removed | Com.asgn _ _ =>
598removed match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
599removed | .const nm _ =>
600removed let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
601removed `(imp_com| $(mkIdent nm):ident := $a;)
602removed | .lit (.strVal s) =>
603removed let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
604removed `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a;)
605removed | _ => `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
606removed | Com.seq _ _ =>
607removed let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabComInner
608removed let s2 ← withAppArg delabComInner
609removed `(imp_com| $s1 $s2)
610removed | Com.cond _ _ _ =>
611removed let b ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
612removed let c1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabComInner
613removed let c2 ← withAppArg delabComInner
614removed `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2})
615removed | Com.whileDo _ _ =>
616removed let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
617removed let c ← withAppArg delabComInner
618removed `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
619removed | _ => `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
620removed annAsTerm stx
621removed
622removed@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
623removed delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
624removedpartial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
625removed guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
626removed | Com.skip => true
627removed | Com.asgn _ _ => true
628removed | Com.seq _ _ => true
629removed | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
630removed | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
631removed | _ => false
632removed match ← delabComInner with
633removed | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
634removed | e => `(term| imp { $e })
635removed
636removedend Imp.Delab
637removed
638removed-- As an example, here is the factorial function again, written as a formal
639removed-- definition. When this command terminates, the variable `Y` will contain the
640removed-- factorial of the initial value of `X`. (Compare this to the concrete Imp
641removed-- program at the very start of the chapter.)
642removed
643removeddef fact_in_lean : Com := imp {
644removed Z := X;
645removed Y := 1;
646removed while (Z ≠ 0) {
647removed Y := Y * Z;
648removed Z := Z - 1;
649removed }
650removed}
651removed
652removed-- Because we registered a delaborator, we can inspect a defined program with
653removed-- `#print`, which pretty prints the stored definition using the same syntax:
654removed
655removed/--
656removedinfo: def fact_in_lean : Com :=
657removedimp {
658removed Z := X;
659removed Y := 1;
660removed while (Z ≠ 0) {
661removed Y := Y * Z;
662removed Z := Z - 1;
663removed }
664removed}
665removed-/
666removed#guard_msgs in
667removed#print fact_in_lean
668removed
669removed-- ### Desugaring Notations
670removed
671removed-- The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
672removed-- convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as when
673removed-- debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax `hide`s the
674removed-- underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we can switch the
675removed-- Imp notation off in Lean's output with `set_option pp.notation false`,
676removed-- which our delaborators honor.
677removed
678removed-- Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded during
679removed-- elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
680removed-- `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that a
681removed-- proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of `Com`,
682removed-- `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal mentions
683removed-- an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and `simp` already
684removed-- act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing to "unfold". The
685removed-- delaborators affect only how that tree is **displayed**. Nevertheless,
686removed-- seeing the raw constructors is sometimes very helpful!
687removed
688removed#check imp { X := X + 1; }
689removed
690removedset_option pp.notation false in
691removed#check imp { X := X + 1; }
692removed
693removed-- ### More Examples
694removed
695removed-- A few more examples.
696removed
697removed-- Assignment:
698removed
699removeddef plus2 : Com := imp { X := X + 2; }
700removeddef XtimesYinZ : Com := imp { Z := X * Y; }
701removed
702removed-- Loops:
703removed
704removeddef subtract_slowly_body : Com := imp {
705removed Z := Z - 1;
706removed X := X - 1;
707removed}
708removed
709removeddef subtract_slowly : Com := imp {
710removed while (X ≠ 0) {
711removed ~subtract_slowly_body
712removed }
713removed}
714removed
715removeddef subtract_3_from_5_slowly : Com := imp {
716removed X := 3;
717removed Z := 5;
718removed ~subtract_slowly
719removed}
720removed
721removed-- An infinite loop:
722removed
723removeddef loop : Com := imp { while (true) { skip; } }
724removed
725removed-- ## Evaluating Commands
726removed
727removed-- Next we need to define what it means to evaluate an Imp command. The fact
728removed-- that `while` loops don't necessarily terminate makes defining an evaluation
729removed-- function tricky.
730removed
731removed-- ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
732removed
733removed-- Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for commands (with a
734removed-- bogus `while` case).
735removed
736removeddef Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
737removed match c with
738removed | imp {skip;} => st
739removed | imp {x := ~a;} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
740removed | imp {~c1 ~c2} =>
741removed let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c1
742removed ceval_fun_no_while st' c2
743removed | imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}} =>
744removed if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c1
745removed else ceval_fun_no_while st c2
746removed | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => st -- bogus
747removed
748removed-- In a more conventional functional language like OCaml or Haskell we could
749removed-- add the `while` case as follows:
750removed
751removed-- | .whileDo b c =>
752removed-- if b.eval st then ceval_fun st (.seq c (.whileDo b c))
753removed-- else st
754removed
755removed-- Lean doesn't accept such a definition ("fail to show termination") because
756removed-- the function we want to define is not guaranteed to terminate. Indeed, it
757removed-- *doesn't* always terminate: the full `ceval_fun` applied to the `loop`
758removed-- program above would run forever. Since Lean aims to be not just a
759removed-- programming language but also a consistent logic, any potentially
760removed-- non-terminating function must be rejected. Here is what would go wrong if
761removed-- Lean allowed non-terminating recursive functions:
762removed
763removed-- def loop_false (n : Nat) : False := loop_false n
764removed
765removed-- That is, propositions like `False` would become provable (`loop_false 0`
766removed-- would be a proof of `False`), a disaster for logical consistency.
767removed
768removed-- Thus, because it doesn't terminate on all inputs, the full `ceval_fun`
769removed-- cannot be written in Lean -- at least not without additional tricks and
770removed-- workarounds.
771removed
772removed-- Note to developers:
773removed-- Perhaps that discussion should be moved to -- or previewed in --
774removed-- Logic.v? MRC'20: It's already in ProofObjects (which not everyone
775removed-- sees).
776removed
777removed-- ### Evaluation as a Relation
778removed
779removed-- Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
780removed-- *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`, similar
781removed-- to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` above.
782removed
783removed-- This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward workarounds,
784removed-- it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For example, if we add
785removed-- nondeterministic features like `any` to the language, we want the
786removed-- definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic -- i.e., not only will it
787removed-- not be total, it will not even be a function!
788removed
789removed-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
790removed-- I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more standard in Lean?
791removed-- CSLib precedent maybe?
792removed
793removed-- We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
794removed-- `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state `st`
795removed-- results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c` takes state
796removed-- `st` to `st'`".
797removed
798removed-- Operational Semantics
799removed
800removed-- Note to developers (before next release):
801removed-- BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with if st' and st''
802removed-- were swapped...
803removed
804removed-- Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference rules
805removed-- for readability:
806removed
807removed-- ----------------- (skip)
808removed-- st =[ skip ]=> st
809removed
810removed-- a.eval st = n
811removed-- -------------------------------- (asgn)
812removed-- st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
813removed
814removed-- st =[ c1 ]=> st'
815removed-- st' =[ c2 ]=> st''
816removed-- --------------------- (seq)
817removed-- st =[ c1;c2 ]=> st''
818removed
819removed-- b.eval st = true
820removed-- st =[ c1 ]=> st'
821removed-- -------------------------------------- (ifTrue)
822removed-- st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
823removed
824removed-- b.eval st = false
825removed-- st =[ c2 ]=> st'
826removed-- -------------------------------------- (ifFalse)
827removed-- st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
828removed
829removed-- b.eval st = false
830removed-- ----------------------------- (whileFalse)
831removed-- st =[ while b do c end ]=> st
832removed
833removed-- b.eval st = true
834removed-- st =[ c ]=> st'
835removed-- st' =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
836removed-- -------------------------------- (whileTrue)
837removed-- st =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
838removed
839removed-- Here is the formal definition. Make sure you understand how it corresponds
840removed-- to the inference rules.
841removed
842removed-- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
843removed-- TODO Propose you use inline notation such as
844removed-- `Com.EvalR (imp {skip;}) st st`
845removed
846removedinductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
847removed | skip (st : State) : EvalR (imp {skip;}) st st
848removed | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
849removed EvalR (imp {x := ~a;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
850removed | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' st'' : State) (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
851removed EvalR (imp {~c1 ~c2}) st st''
852removed | ifTrue (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
853removed (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
854removed EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
855removed | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
856removed (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
857removed EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
858removed | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
859removed EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st
860removed | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
861removed (hc : EvalR c st st') (hloop : Com.EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'') :
862removed EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st''
863removed
864removednotation:40 st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 => Com.EvalR c st0 st1
865removed-- Also accept a bare Imp command between the brackets, so concrete programs can
866removed-- be written without the `imp { … }` wrapper. Bare `Com` terms still work via the
867removed-- notation above; splice a Lean term into the command with `~`.
868removedsyntax:40 term:41 " =[ " imp_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
869removedmacro_rules
870removed | `($st0 =[ $c:imp_com ]=> $st1) => `($st0 =[ imp { $c } ]=> $st1)
871removed
872removed-- The cost of defining evaluation as a relation instead of a function is that
873removed-- we now need to construct a *proof* that some program evaluates to some
874removed-- result state, rather than letting Lean's computation mechanism do it for
875removed-- us.
876removed
877removedexample :
878removed ∅ =[
879removed X := 2;
880removed if (X ≤ 1) {
881removed Y := 3;
882removed } else {
883removed Z := 4;
884removed }
885removed ]=> (Z →ₜ 4 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
886removed -- We must supply the intermediate state.
887removed apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
888removed · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
889removed · apply Com.EvalR.ifFalse
890removed · rfl
891removed · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
892removed

897removed X := 0;
898removed Y := 1;
899removed Z := 2;
900removed ]=> (Z →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 1 ; X →ₜ 0 ; ∅) := by

904removed-- PR: I phrased these quizzes with the following alternatives: (A) Not
905removed-- true (B) True and easily provable (C) True and takes more work to prove
906removed-- (D) True and cannot be proved without additional axioms

908removed-- _Quiz:_
909removed

911removed
912removed-- ∀ (c : Com) (st st' : State),
913removed-- st =[ skip; ~c ]=> st' →
914removed-- st =[ c ]=> st'
915removed
916removed-- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure
917removed

919removed
920removed-- Is the following proposition provable?
921removed
922removed-- ∀ (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' : State),
923removed-- st =[ ~c1 ~c2 ]=> st' →
924removed-- st =[ c1 ]=> st →
925removed-- st =[ c2 ]=> st'
926removed
927removed-- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure

930removed
931removed-- Is the following proposition provable?
932removed
933removed-- ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st st' : State),
934removed-- st =[ if (~b) { ~c } else { ~c } ]=> st' →
935removed-- st =[ c ]=> st'

939removed-- _Quiz:_
940removed
941removed-- Is the following proposition provable?
942removed
943removed-- ∀ (b : Bexp),
944removed-- (∀ st, b.eval st = true) →
945removed-- ∀ (c : Com) (st : State),
946removed-- ¬ ∃ st', st =[ while (~b) { ~c } ]=> st'
947removed
948removed-- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure

950removed-- _Quiz:_
951removed
952removed-- Is the following proposition provable?
953removed
954removed-- ∀ (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (st : State),
955removed-- (¬ ∃ st', st =[ while (~b) { ~c } ]=> st') →
956removed-- ∀ st'', b.eval st'' = true
957removed
958removed-- (A) Yes (B) No (C) Not sure
959removed
960removed-- ### Determinism of Evaluation
961removed
962removed-- Changing from a computational to a relational definition of evaluation is a
963removed-- good move because it frees us from the artificial requirement that
964removed-- evaluation be a total function. But it raises a question: is the relational
965removed-- definition really a partial *function*? Could the same command, from the
966removed-- same state, evaluate to two different final states? In fact this cannot
967removed-- happen: `ceval` *is* a partial function.
968removed
969removedtheorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
970removed (e1 : st =[ c ]=> st1) (e2 : st =[ c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
971removed induction e1 generalizing st2 with
972removed | skip st =>
973removed cases e2 with
974removed | skip => rfl
975removed | asgn st a n x h =>
976removed cases e2 with
977removed | asgn _ _ n' _ h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
978removed | seq c1 c2 st st' st'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
979removed cases e2 with
980removed | seq _ _ _ st2' _ h1' h2' =>
981removed have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ h1'
982removed subst hst
983removed exact ih2 _ h2'
984removed | ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
985removed cases e2 with
986removed | ifTrue _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
987removed | ifFalse _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => simp_all
988removed | ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
989removed cases e2 with

991removed | ifFalse _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
992removed | whileFalse b st c hb =>
993removed cases e2 with
994removed | whileFalse _ _ _ hb' => rfl
995removed | whileTrue _ _ _ _ _ hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
996removed | whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
997removed cases e2 with
998removed | whileFalse _ _ _ hb' => simp_all
999removed | whileTrue _ st2' _ _ _ hb' hc' hl' =>
1000removed have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ hc'

1004removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): pup_to_n ⭐⭐⭐
1005removed
1006removed-- Write an Imp program that sums the numbers from `1` to `X` (inclusive) in
1007removed-- the variable `Y`. Your program should update the state as shown in
1008removed-- `pup_to_2_ceval`, which you can reverse-engineer to discover the program
1009removed-- you should write. The proof of that theorem will be somewhat lengthy.
1010removed
1011removeddef pup_to_n : Com := sorry
1012removed
1013removedtheorem pup_to_2_ceval :
1014removed (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ pup_to_n ]=>
1015removed (X →ₜ 0 ; Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 1 ; Y →ₜ 2 ; Y →ₜ 0 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
1016removed sorry

1018removed-- ## Reasoning About Imp Programs
1019removed
1020removed-- We'll get into more systematic and powerful techniques for reasoning about
1021removed-- Imp programs in the next chapter, but we can already do a few things
1022removed-- (albeit in a somewhat low-level way) just by working with the bare
1023removed-- definitions. This section explores some examples.
1024removed
1025removedtheorem plus2_spec (st : State) (n : Nat) (st' : State)
1026removed (hx : st[X] = n) (heval : st =[ plus2 ]=> st') :
1027removed st'[X] = n + 2 := by
1028removed -- Inverting `heval` forces one step of the `ceval` computation: since
1029removed -- `plus2` is an assignment, `st'` must be `st` extended at `X`.
1030removed unfold plus2 at heval
1031removed cases heval with
1032removed | asgn _ _ m _ h =>
1033removed simp only [Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num] at h
1034removed rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1035removed lia

1048removed-- equation).

1054removed
1055removed-- The following function yields `true` just on programs with no while loops.
1056removed-- Using `inductive`, write a property `Com.NoWhilesR` that holds exactly when

1058removed

1060removed match c with
1061removed | imp {skip;} => true
1062removed | imp {_x := ~_a;} => true
1063removed | imp {~c1 ~c2} => no_whiles c1 && no_whiles c2
1064removed | imp {if (~_) {~ct} else {~cf}} => no_whiles ct && no_whiles cf
1065removed | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => false

1067removedinductive Com.NoWhilesR : Com → Prop where
1068removed -- FILL IN HERE

1070removedtheorem no_whiles_eqv (c : Com) : c.no_whiles = true ↔ Com.NoWhilesR c := by

1080removed ∃ st', st =[ c ]=> st' := by

11removed-- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12removed-- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13removed-- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14removed-- through spanshot tasks.
15removedprivate def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16removed match (← get).scopes with
17removed | [] => act
18removed | h :: t =>
19removed let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20removed try
21removed orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23removed act
24removed finally
25removed if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26removed let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27removed modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28removed
29removedprivate def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30removed let savedState ← get
31removed try
32removed m
33removed finally
34removed let state ← get
35removed set { savedState with
36removed -- Preserve the info tree
37removed infoState := state.infoState
38removed messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39removed
40removednamespace IndentedCommands
41removed
42removed/-! # Block Commands Parser
43removed Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44removed Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45removed we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46removed because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47removed One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48removed and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49removed-/
50removed
51removedopen Parser
52removed
53removedprivate def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54removed eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55removed
56removed/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57removedprivate def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58removed takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59removed
60removed/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61removed If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62removed requiring the indentation.
63removed-/
64removedprivate def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65removed takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66removed (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67removed (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68removed
69removedprivate def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70removed rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71removed
72removedprivate def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73removed
74removed@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76removed
77removed@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78removedprivate def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79removed
80removedprivate partial def runRawCmdsAux
81removed (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82removed let state ← get
83removed let scope := state.scopes.head!
84removed let pctx := {
85removed env := state.env
86removed options := scope.opts
87removed currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88removed openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89removed }
90removed let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91removed modify fun state => { state with messages }
92removed unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93removed elabCommand cmd
94removed runLinters cmd
95removed unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96removed runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97removed
98removed/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99removedprivate def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100removed let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101removed | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102removed let fileName ← getFileName
103removed let fileMap ← getFileMap
104removed -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105removed -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106removed -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107removed let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108removed if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109removed let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110removed (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111removed runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112removed else
113removed throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114removed
115removedend IndentedCommands
116removed
117removedend
118removed
119removedpublic meta section
120removed
121removedopen Parser IndentedCommands
122removed
123removed/--
124removedElaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125removedbut discards their effects afterwards.

135removeddef experimentTk := leading_parser
136removed "sf_experiment"

138removed@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139removed experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140removed checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141removed
142removed/--
143removedSucceeds only if the enclosed commands fail.

145removed
146removedExample:

149removed example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150removed```
151removed-/
152removeddef expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153removed "sf_expect_failure"
154removed
155removed/-
156removed Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
157removed-/
158removeddef expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159removed "sf_expect_failure?"
160removed
161removed@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162removed expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163removed checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164removed
165removed@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166removed expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167removed checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168removed
169removed@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170removeddef elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171removed let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172removed commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173removed runRawCmds body
174removed
175removed@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176removeddef elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177removed let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178removed unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179removed throwUnsupportedSyntax
180removed let tk := stx[0]
181removed let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182removed commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183removed withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184removed
185removedend
